newsitem.title: RUSSIA: New violence rocks Russia before Chechnya talks.
newsitem.headline: New violence rocks Russia before Chechnya talks.

text.p: Unidentified gunmen shot dead a local official in southern Russia on Wednesday, further stoking tensions in the volatile region after a series of violent acts blamed on Chechen separatists.
President Boris Yeltsin, who is vacationing at the Black Sea resort of Sochi, was meeting Interior Minister Anatoly Kulikov to discuss security measures on Russia's southern rim.

Itar-Tass news agency quoted Boris Agapov, vice-president of the ethnic republic of Ingushetia, which borders Chechnya, as saying the attackers killed the region's Deputy Interior Minister Khamzat Dzeitov and his driver as they drove a suspected criminal to prison. The prisoner escaped.
The situation around Chechnya, where 21 months of war between Moscow troops and rebels ended in a shaky truce in August, has deteriorated badly over the past week.
Interfax news agency quoted Russian security sources as saying police had found and disarmed two car bombs on Wednesday in Ingushetia's capital, Nazran.
On Tuesday Russian police fought a brief pre-dawn skirmish with a group of what they said were 20 Chechen fighters just outside Chechnya, resulting in casualties on both sides.
A day earlier two people were killed and more that 20 wounded in an explosion at the railway station in the southern Russian spa resort of Pyatigorsk.

Chechen and Russian officials expressed fears the violence would disrupt peace talks, but on Wednesday senior Yeltsin aide Boris Berezovsky and presidential chief of staff Ivan Rybkin flew to the Chechen capital of Grozny to meet the separatists.
Tass quoted Rybkin as saying at Grozny airport that there were forces aiming at maintaining hostility around Chechnya on both sides and urged joint efforts to neutralise these forces.
"Many people in Chechnya and in Russia want to disrupt the fragile peace, but we shall block such attempts," Rybkin said.
Kulikov said on Tuesday that two Chechen women fighters, seized after the Pyatigorsk blast, had admitted planting a device.

His accusations were immediately denied by Chechen Deputy Prime Minister Movladi Udugov, Itar-Tass said. The separatist leaders accused unnamed Russian special services of planting the bomb to disrupt peacemaking.
Chechen Vice-President Vakha Arsanov, quoted by Interfax, said talks on political matters were impossible until Kulikov apologised for his allegations or proved them.

Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin made clear on Tuesday that Moscow did not want the latest violence to disrupt talks on a long-term peace deal with Chechnya, which must set out whether the region is part of Russia or independent.

"Our views on the (peace) treaty will not be affected by this...the Chechen leadership has denied any connection with these terrorist attacks," Chernomyrdin told a news conference in the Slovak capital Bratislava.
Tass quoted Yeltsin's spokesman Sergei Yastrzhembsky as saying the Kremlin leader had urged Kulikov to focus on preventing such incidents in the future.
